lessons.title: The Real Cost of Each: The Interest Tax Shield vs the Hidden Cost of Equity

children.text: Ask a founder which is cheaper, a 10% loan or equity that pays no dividend at all, and most will say the equity. It is the most expensive mistake in corporate finance, and it survives because the cost of debt arrives as a bank entry while the cost of equity never arrives at all.
This lesson puts real numbers on both sides, including the one genuine subsidy the tax system gives to borrowing.

body.text: Debt is cheaper than equity twice over: lenders demand less because they are paid first, and the government pays part of the interest bill by allowing the deduction. Neither of those applies to equity.

children.text: The Interest Tax Shield

Interest is a business expense. It is deducted before profit is taxed, so a company that borrows pays less tax than an identical company that does not. Dividends get no such treatment: they are paid out of profit that has already been taxed.

In India this deduction sits in Section 32(1)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [previously Section 36(1)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961], which allows interest paid on capital borrowed for the purposes of the business. One condition catches companies out: interest on money borrowed to acquire an asset is not deductible for the period from borrowing until that asset is first put to use.

body.caption: The tax the company does not pay, purely because it borrowed

body.label: What an Indian company actually pays in tax
body.value: About 25.17% under the concessional corporate regime
body.context: The headline rate of 22% for domestic companies opting into the concessional regime becomes roughly 25.17% once the 10% surcharge and 4% cess are applied: 22% times 1.10 times 1.04. Newer manufacturing companies can access a lower rate, and companies outside the concessional regime pay more. Use your own effective rate, not the headline one, in any of the calculations below.

body.caption: A 10% loan is not a 10% cost to a taxpaying company

body.title: What the loan really costs
body.prompt: A profitable Indian company borrows at 10% a year and pays tax at an effective rate of 25.17%. What is its after-tax cost of debt, in percent? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 10% times (1 minus 0.2517) is 7.48%. The government effectively funds about a quarter of the interest bill through the deduction. Against equity investors expecting 14% or more, the gap is far wider than the headline rates suggest.

body.text: The shield is worthless if there is no tax to shield. A loss-making company gets no benefit this year, because there is no taxable profit to reduce. Losses can generally be carried forward and set off in later years subject to conditions, so the benefit is deferred rather than destroyed, but a startup burning cash should never include a tax shield in its comparison of debt against equity.

body.title: Why one is cheaper
body.textWithBlank: Interest is deducted before profit is taxed, while dividends are paid out of ___ profit.
body.explanation: This asymmetry is the tax shield. It is the only place in corporate finance where the government subsidises one funding choice over the other.

children.text: The Hidden Cost of Equity
Equity has no invoice, so its cost has to be reasoned out. There are three parts, and each is larger than founders expect.
The expected return.
Shareholders want 14% or more from a listed company, and far more from a private one. Fail to deliver and the share price or the next round's valuation pays for it.
Permanent dilution.
A slice sold today is a slice of every rupee the company earns forever. Debt is repaid and gone. Equity never is.
Control and process costs.
Board seats, consent rights, reporting obligations and the time senior management spends managing shareholders.

The second one is the killer, and it is easy to quantify. Suppose a founder sells 20% to raise ₹10 crore today. Fifteen years later the company earns ₹80 crore a year. That 20% is now a claim on ₹16 crore of annual profit, permanently, against a one-time ₹10 crore that a loan would have returned in full years earlier.

columns.label: A ₹10 crore loan at 10%
points: Interest of ₹1 crore a year, falling as it amortises
After tax, roughly ₹75 lakh a year
Repaid in full over the tenure, then the cost stops
Lender has no claim on future growth
Must be serviced even in a bad year

columns.label: ₹10 crore of equity for 20%
points: No tax deduction, because there is nothing to deduct
Never repaid, so the claim never ends
A fifth of the company transferred permanently
Investor shares in every rupee of future growth
Nothing owed in a bad year, which is its real advantage

body.text: Read the last line of each column together. Equity is expensive precisely because of the one thing it does well: it never forces a payment. You are buying insurance against bad years, and the premium is a permanent share of the good ones.

children.text: Putting Them Together: WACC
Most companies use both, so the cost of capital is a blend. The
weighted average cost of capital
weights the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity by how much of each the company uses.

markDefs.definition: The blended cost of all the money in a business, weighting the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity by how much of each the company uses. Shortened to WACC.

body.caption: D is debt, E is equity, Kd the pre-tax cost of debt, Ke the cost of equity and T the tax rate

body.title: Blend the two
body.prompt: A company funds itself 40% with debt costing 10% before tax and 60% with equity costing 14.2%. Its effective tax rate is 25.17%. What is its WACC, in percent? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: The after-tax cost of debt is 10% times (1 minus 0.2517), which is 7.48%. Then 0.40 times 7.48% is 2.99%, and 0.60 times 14.2% is 8.52%. Together that is 11.51%. Every project this company funds needs to beat 11.51% to create value.

body.text: WACC is the number that connects fundraising to operations. It is the hurdle rate for every investment decision the company makes. Change the funding mix and you change the hurdle, which changes which projects are worth doing.

children.text: So Why Not Borrow Everything?
If debt is cheaper and tax-deductible, the obvious conclusion is to fund the company almost entirely with it. Every over-leveraged corporate failure in India is a version of that reasoning.

Two things break it. First, lenders raise their price as leverage rises, because their own risk rises. Second, shareholders demand more too, because the equity underneath a large debt pile is far riskier. Add
financial distress
costs and the blended cost eventually turns upward.

markDefs.definition: The costs that appear as a company becomes visibly over-borrowed: higher interest, nervous suppliers, lost customers, management time spent on lenders rather than the business.

body.title: Illustrative cost of capital as leverage rises (%)
body.xAxisLabel: Debt as a share of total capital (%)

children.text: The WACC line falls, flattens and then rises. The bottom of that curve is the theoretically optimal capital structure. In practice nobody can locate it precisely, which is why sensible companies aim for a comfortable range rather than an exact point, and keep headroom for a bad year.

body.text: The curve above is illustrative, not a model of any real company. Its shape is the lesson, not its numbers. The right leverage for a business depends on how stable its cash flows are, and a company with volatile revenue should sit far to the left of one with contracted, predictable income.

body.title: Why the tax shield argument is weaker than textbooks suggest

children.text: The tax shield is real, but four things reduce it in practice.
No profit, no shield.
Loss-making companies get nothing today, only a carried-forward benefit subject to conditions.
Interest on an asset under construction
is not deductible until the asset is first put to use, which delays the benefit on exactly the large capex borrowings where it would matter most.
Thin capitalisation limits.

Indian tax law caps the interest deduction available on certain borrowings from associated enterprises, which restricts groups from loading an Indian entity with related-party debt purely for the deduction.
Distress costs arrive earlier than the textbook curve suggests.
Suppliers shorten credit, customers hesitate on long contracts, and good employees leave, all well before any formal default.
The practical conclusion: take the shield as a genuine advantage of debt, not as a reason to maximise debt.

body.title: Does the shield apply?
body.question: A three-year-old Bengaluru SaaS company is loss-making and expects to remain so for two more years. A venture debt fund offers ₹8 crore at 15%. How should the company evaluate the cost of that debt?
options: At 15% times (1 minus the tax rate), because interest is always deductible
At the full 15%, because there is no taxable profit to shield this year
At zero, because startups do not pay tax
At 15% plus the cost of equity
body.explanation: The deduction only helps a company that is paying tax. With no taxable profit, the after-tax and pre-tax cost are the same 15% today. The unabsorbed loss may be carried forward subject to conditions, so some benefit may arrive later, but pricing the debt at 11.2% today would simply be wrong.

body.title: Which decision creates value?
body.question: A company with a WACC of 11.5% is considering two projects. Project A returns 10.5% and Project B returns 13%. Both are the same risk as the existing business. What should it do?
options: Do both, since both are profitable
Do only Project B, because Project A returns less than the cost of the capital funding it
Do only Project A, because it is cheaper
Neither, because WACC is only relevant to fundraising
body.explanation: Project A earns 10.5% on money that costs 11.5%, destroying about 1 percentage point of value a year even though the accounts will show a profit. Project B clears the hurdle. This is the entire practical purpose of knowing your cost of capital.

body.title: The board asks for a recommendation
body.scenario: You are the finance head of a profitable Coimbatore textile machinery company. Revenue is ₹340 crore, EBITDA ₹48 crore, existing debt ₹60 crore at an average 9.5%, and net worth ₹180 crore. The company pays tax at an effective 25.17%. It needs ₹80 crore for a new assembly line with an expected return of about 16% a year. A bank will lend the full ₹80 crore at 10%, secured on the new line. A private equity investor will provide ₹80 crore of equity for 18% of the company, which shareholders believe is worth more than that.
body.prompt: Prepare the comparison the board needs.
body.modelAnswer:
Start with cost:
1. The loan costs 10% before tax, 7.48% after the Section 32(1)(b) deduction. On ₹80 crore that is ₹8 crore of interest a year, about ₹5.99 crore after tax.
2. The equity costs nothing in cash and 18% of everything the company earns forever. If the company sustains ₹48 crore of EBITDA and grows, 18% of that stream is worth far more over a decade than ₹60 crore of cumulative after-tax interest. Say so in rupees, not in principle, because that is the comparison the board will remember.
3. The project returns 16%, comfortably above both the after-tax cost of debt and any reasonable WACC. The project is worth doing either way. The question is purely how to fund it.

Then test whether the company can carry the debt:
4. Post-borrowing debt is ₹140 crore against EBITDA of ₹48 crore, which is about 2.9x. That is within the range most Indian lenders accept for a manufacturer, but it is not conservative.
5. Interest would rise from about ₹5.7 crore to ₹13.7 crore, giving interest coverage of roughly 3.5x on current EBITDA before the new line contributes. Stress it: if EBITDA fell 30% to ₹33.6 crore, coverage drops to about 2.5x and debt to EBITDA rises above 4x, which would breach typical covenants.
6. Debt to net worth moves from 0.33 to 0.78. Check the existing loan documents for any covenant capping this.

Recommendation:
7. Fund it with debt, but not necessarily all of it in one go. Borrow against the asset with a tenure matched to its life, keep some headroom, and consider a modest promoter or internal accrual contribution to keep debt to EBITDA below 2.5x.
8. Selling 18% of a profitable company to fund one assembly line is the most expensive financing available here, and it is permanent. Equity is the right answer when the outcome is uncertain. This outcome is not: the line has a known return and a saleable asset behind it.
9. Bring the downside case to the board yourself. A recommendation to borrow is only credible when it comes with the number that would make it wrong.

body.title: Comparing the true cost of any two funding offers
steps: Convert the debt cost to after-tax using your own effective tax rate, not the headline rate
Confirm the company will actually be paying tax in the years the interest is paid
Check whether the interest is deductible now or only once the asset is put to use
Express the equity cost as a share of expected future profits, not just as today's valuation
Add fees, guarantees and covenant costs to the debt side
Add board, reporting and consent obligations to the equity side
Recalculate WACC after the raise, and check the project still clears it
Stress the interest cover and debt to EBITDA against a bad year before committing

cards.definition: Tax saved because interest is deducted before profit is taxed. Interest times the effective tax rate.
The provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025 allowing deduction of interest on capital borrowed for business, formerly Section 36(1)(iii) of the 1961 Act.
Headline rate plus surcharge and cess. About 25.17% under the 22% concessional corporate regime.
Interest rate times one minus the tax rate.
The return shareholders expect. No deduction, no repayment, no end date.
The blended cost of debt and equity, weighted by how much of each the company uses.
The return a project must beat to create value, usually the WACC for same-risk projects.
The rising costs of being visibly over-borrowed, well before any formal default.

points: Debt is cheaper than equity because lenders are paid first and because interest is tax deductible.
In India that deduction sits in Section 32(1)(b) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly Section 36(1)(iii) of the 1961 Act.
At an effective tax rate of about 25.17%, a 10% loan costs roughly 7.48% after tax.
The tax shield is worth nothing to a loss-making company in the year it is claimed.
Equity costs no cash but transfers a permanent share of all future profits, which is why it is the most expensive capital available.
WACC blends both and becomes the hurdle rate for every investment decision the company takes.
Cheap debt stops being cheap as leverage rises, because both lenders and shareholders reprice the risk.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Tax rates, surcharge and cess change with each Finance Act, and the treatment of any specific borrowing depends on facts and conditions not covered here. The cost of capital curve is illustrative. Consult a qualified chartered accountant on any actual tax position.
